title: Credit card delinquency is easing unevenly as pandemic accounts age
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: The rise in US credit card delinquency after 2022 was particularly large in lower-income neighbourhoods. New York Fed researchers link part of the pattern to a group of accounts opened in 2020–22, when new cards reached borrowers with lower origination scores. As these accounts age, their contribution to new serious delinquency is declining. The authors expect some further improvement if macroeconomic conditions hold up and newer lending remains of higher quality. Their argument concerns the changing composition of outstanding cards. It coexists with a gap in payment performance between neighbourhoods that remained wider in 2026 than before the pandemic.

The delinquency measure tracks balances crossing into arrears of at least 90 days. Its denominator is balances that were not already seriously delinquent in the previous quarter, and the chart reports a four-quarter moving sum. The groups are equal-population quartiles of average adjusted gross income in borrowers’ ZIP codes, so neighbourhood income is a proxy for a borrower’s circumstances. In the data accompanying Chart 1, the measure for the lowest-income quartile fell from 7.99% in 2019 Q4 to 5.08% in 2021 Q4, then reached 10.33% in 2026 Q3. The comparable readings for the highest quartile were 3.57%, 2.18% and 4.40%. The difference between the two groups had widened to 5.93 percentage points by 2026 Q3. These are balance-weighted transitions. They do not show the fraction of all people in an income group missing a payment.

The authors view the macroeconomic environment as the likely main driver of the initial improvement and subsequent deterioration. Forbearance, transfers and lower consumption helped households pay during the pandemic. Inflation and borrowing costs subsequently increased pressure as support expired. The composition of lending may also have mattered. Relief arrangements kept some past-due episodes off credit records and the population’s scores rose. Meanwhile, the shares of newly issued cards and newly extended limits going to borrowers in the lowest-income neighbourhoods each increased by nearly two percentage points at the start of the pandemic and remained elevated until 2023. These observations are consistent with some easing of underwriting. They cannot by themselves establish a change in approval criteria independent of changes in applications (Charts 2–3).

The median origination score averaged 688 in 2020–22 against 699 in 2017–19, even as scores in the broader population were improving. Many of these pandemic accounts encountered difficult conditions early in their lives, when unseasoned accounts have historically carried greater delinquency risk. The 2017–19 cohort experienced the same age profile under more favourable pandemic conditions. Chart 4 separates vintage contributions using the eligible balances across all vintages as a common denominator. In 2026 Q3 the 2020–22 group contributed about 1.80 percentage points, below its roughly 2.87 points in 2024 Q4; the 2023–25 group contributed about 2.61 points in 2026 Q3. This shift incorporates changing outstanding balances, seasoning and selection among surviving accounts. It cannot be read as a standalone default rate for each cohort.

Card scores at origination in 2025 were below 2024 levels but remained above the pre-pandemic and pandemic averages discussed in the paper. The article’s separate household-debt context extends to 2026 Q3; the accompanying origination-score series ends in 2025 Q4. The authors’ conditional optimism therefore turns on both the quality of more recent originations and the economic environment those accounts face. Stable aggregate non-housing transitions in the latest quarterly debt report can conceal large differences across neighbourhoods, lenders’ origination years and the vulnerable borrowers within each.

questions.question: How much of the falling pandemic-vintage contribution reflects better payment performance on comparable balances?
questions.detail: Chart 4 divides by balances across vintages, while the number and composition of surviving accounts change. Projecting losses for a lender requires within-vintage transitions and balances at matched account ages. Use the credit panel and issuer disclosures to distinguish paydowns, closed or charged-off accounts and genuine improvements among comparable surviving borrowers.

questions.question: Did approval standards change after accounting for who applied and how relief affected reported scores?
questions.detail: The article observes lower origination scores while population scores generally rose, and a larger share of new lending to lower-income areas. It does not observe lenders’ decisions on otherwise comparable applications. Seek approval-rate and credit-limit evidence conditional on application characteristics, relief status and issuer. Differentiating a supply shift from a changing applicant pool matters for evaluating the risk of newer lending.

questions.question: Is more recent underwriting sufficient to offset a worsening macroeconomic environment?
questions.detail: The authors’ outlook assumes no major macro shock, and the score chart ends in 2025. Assess the exposure of the latest vintages by combining updated origination and early arrears data with local income and employment conditions. Compare outcomes within ZIP-code groups as well as across them. Neighbourhood averages alone cannot establish which borrowers have the weakest cash buffers.
